A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices A–F support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM evaluations, an expert food-scientist study, and randomized menu evaluations involving 552 participants.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and reports additional expert comparisons, menu conditions, and statistical analyses.

M1.justification: The proposed framework still generates candidate recipes, estimates preferences with an LLM, and selects a menu through integer quadratic programming. Its objective, constraints, and main components remain unchanged. Removing objective components is introduced as ablation testing.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four tasks using NECTAR, Food.com, the 58-pair Epicurious evaluation set, and the same restaurant-menu setting and target populations. Added comparison arms and illustrative recipe pairs remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds an Expert Chef menu and a Beef to Chicken baseline to the menu comparison (Table 13), plus an expert food scientist for overall-satisfaction prediction (Table 14). These substantially extend comparisons beyond v1's existing LLM, nutritional, random-choice, and menu baselines.

E3.justification: The menu evaluation expands from 11 to 16 conditions, including controls that remove preference and diversity objectives, and reports 800 participants instead of 552. Existing populations and metrics are retained. However, Table 7 still lists only the original 552 participants, leaving allocation to the added arms undocumented.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate removals of the preference objective, diversity objective, and both objectives, directly testing their contributions to menu outcomes (Table 13 and Figures 16–25). Table 10 also adds sensitivity analysis across statistical tests for the experimental-design study. Existing quartile, dietary-subgroup, and description-removal analyses remain.

E5.justification: For the expert experimental-design comparison, v2 supplements v1's t-test with paired t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, an evaluator random-effects model, permutation tests, and adjusted OLS (Table 10). This substantially broadens treatment of dependence and distributional assumptions. Existing confidence-interval reporting remains; additional LLM runs or seeds are not documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds five menu-condition result rows, expert sensory-prediction accuracies, and statistical-sensitivity results. For example, the new Expert Chef and Beef to Chicken menus report emissions of 41.28 and 17.57 kg CO2eq/kg, respectively; the sensory expert achieves 0.65 overall accuracy. Retained table values and plotted means are unchanged. v1's 70% overall prediction accuracy for the description-removal variant is omitted, while its 84% highest-quartile result remains.

T1.justification: Proposition 6.1 tightens the error bound from 2Kε + 2λD to 2Kε. Appendix A correspondingly removes the unnecessary diversity-dependent terms from the proof. The optimization definitions, assumptions, and underlying proof argument remain.

C1.justification: The main contributions remain the task typology, four-task LLM evaluation, and optimization-augmented menu framework. The headline claims of 45% versus 22% estimated time savings and 79% emissions reduction while maintaining satisfaction are retained.

C2.justification: The substantive interpretations concerning coarse-grained prediction, omnivore bias, and optimization remain. The explanation involving recipe titles versus descriptions is retained in v2 Table 11. The limitations remain substantively unchanged, including statements treating expert baselines as future work despite the added comparisons.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, discloses the new experts' experience and coauthor status, defines the objective-removal conditions, and supplies their menus in Appendix F. Existing prompts and main hyperparameters remain unchanged. Reproducibility documentation is incomplete for the additional participants and study arms.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds Jiang et al.'s LLMOpt and a data-driven optimization paragraph citing Bertsimas and Kallus and Elmachtoub and Grigas. It explicitly positions the framework as extending predict-then-optimize through candidate generation and LLM-based prediction; the broader positioning remains.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized corrections and clarifications, including fixing 'capabi,' explaining preference gaps and order frequency, and illustrating menu-item descriptions. Short passages accompany the additions, but the main narrative and section organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds three recipe-pair example figures and two analytical tables, expands the menu-results table, and redraws ten appendix charts to include five additional arms with expanded labels and captions. These substantially extend the displayed comparisons, while the two main figures retain their graphical content.

improvement.justification: The objective ablations and alternative statistical tests address gaps in v1's support for its menu framework and expert-design findings. Expert comparisons, the tighter bound, and code-access information also help. The gain is limited by incomplete integration: Table 7 still accounts for 552 participants despite the reported 800, added-arm procedures are underdescribed, and limitations still present added expert baselines as future work.
